idiom_name: single explicit boolean access yielding the native boolean (explicit conversion or named predicate)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: expose exactly one way to ask the yes/no question, and make it yield the language's own boolean - an explicit conversion operator where user-defined conversions exist (C++ `explicit operator bool`, C# `operator true`/`operator false`, Python `__bool__`), otherwise a named predicate such as `isEmpty()`/`isValid()` returning the native boolean type. Never let the test value be an integer, pointer or enum that participates in arithmetic or ordering: in C and C++ an implicit conversion to bool promotes to int, so `x + 1`, `x < 42`, `int i = x` and deletion through the conversion all become legal and silently change meaning. Keep the conversion out of comparisons with numbers and out of comparisons between unrelated testable types (make those compile errors), and keep the boolean result out of arithmetic on the caller side (in C and Python the boolean is itself an integer). Where the question is ambiguous or multiple (valid, empty, at end, no error), prefer named predicates over one overloaded truth test.
code_sketch:
testable:                                  # value with one clear validity question
    boolean_access() -> native boolean     # explicit conversion or predicate

if testable.boolean_access(): ...          # allowed: if / while / ! / && / || / ternary
# testable + 1                             # rejected: no arithmetic on the test
# testable < 42                            # rejected: no ordering
# testable_a == testable_b                 # rejected: unrelated testables stay incomparable
pitfalls: If the boolean access is implicit, every context that accepts the target type accepts the object: overload resolution changes, unrelated types become comparable through the shared conversion, and the result can promote to an integer type.
A single truth test cannot express several questions; different readers assign different meanings to the same object (iostreams: does `if (s)` include eofbit?).
The restriction is compile-time and covers accidental paths only: explicit casts and the language's own coercions (C's _Bool promotion, Python's bool being an int) still escape it.
Wrapping the conversion in a framework or generic wrapper without restating the question hides it behind yet another layer.

Wrong move: write `operator bool` implicit so templates and overload sets 'just work' -> the conversion becomes visible to every context that accepts bool or promotes from it: `int i = x`, `obj << 1`, `obj < 42` and comparisons between two unrelated testable types compile, and the test result promotes to int -> instead mark it `explicit`; contextual conversion to bool already admits the value in `if`, `while`, `!`, `&&`, `||` and ternary conditions, so implicitness buys nothing but damage.

Wrong move: after replacing the pointer-to-member realisation with `explicit operator bool`, keep legacy `if (p == 0)` code compiling by re-adding a numeric conversion or an `operator==` against integrals -> every type reachable through that conversion is orderable and comparable with numbers again, silently restoring the bug class the idiom exists to eliminate -> instead add `nullptr_t` comparison overloads for the legitimate sentinel and rewrite the call sites as `if (p)`.

Wrong move: treat language truthiness as the end state - return `int` status sentinels from predicates, or lean on the fact that every object is truthy (JavaScript) or that `bool` subclasses `int` (Python `True + 1 == 2`) -> the misuse merely relocates from the conversion to the raw value, and `if (result == 1)` / `total += result` spread through the codebase -> instead expose exactly one named test returning the language's native boolean and keep numbers out of the API entirely.
